DEU.story:
In 1961 Paul Schäfer, a former Nazi army corporal wanted in Germany on child abuse charges, left for southern Chile and founded a commune called Colonia Dignidad. The colony drew children from local farms into its free school and clinic. In 1966 a teenager who had fled the colony took refuge at the West German embassy; the embassy sent a delegation, said it found no evidence, and German diplomats went on calling it a "model colony". Chilean officials believe the colony was used to torture opponents of the Pinochet dictatorship from 1973 to 1990. An investigation opened only after Chilean mothers complained in 1997. In 2006 a Chilean court sentenced Schäfer to 20 years for sexually abusing 25 children. In April 2016 Foreign Minister Frank-Walter Steinmeier said German diplomats had "at best looked away" from the 60s to the 80s, and in 2017 the Bundestag acknowledged German responsibility. The colony's doctor, Hartmut Hopp, convicted in Chile in 2011 of aiding the abuse, was living in Germany when the German investigation into him was dropped in 2019.

Inside Germany, officials did some of the placing themselves. From the late 1960s West Berlin's youth authorities, on the advice of the sexologist Helmut Kentler, placed homeless boys with men known to be paedophiles as foster fathers. A University of Hildesheim report in 2024 traced a nationwide network that tolerated this beyond 2000. Kentler died in 2008 without prosecution. One name in that network, Gerold Becker, was headmaster of the Odenwaldschule, where at least 132 pupils were abused from the 1960s to the 1990s. Pupils reported it in 1998, a newspaper published it in 1999, a promised review never happened, and prosecutors dropped the case because the legal deadline had passed. It came out only in 2010. Becker died that year without facing legal consequences. The same pattern of moving, not stopping, shows in the church: Fr Peter Hullermann was sent from Essen to Munich in 1980 for therapy, given pastoral work, and abused again. A 2018 study commissioned by the bishops counted 1,670 clerics accused of abusing 3,677 minors and found personnel files destroyed or manipulated.

2010 became the turning point. After the Canisius-Kolleg revelations that January, the government set up a Round Table and an Independent Commissioner. In 2013 the Bundestag lengthened the deadline to sue from 3 to 30 years, though not for claims that had already expired.

Germany is also a destination and a hub. Korean children (2,352 from 1965 to 1996) and Sri Lankan babies from the 1980s "baby farms" were adopted into German families. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation acted on 18,401 web addresses of abuse material hosted in Germany, 6% of its total. German police seized the Kidflix streaming server in 2025, leading to 1,393 suspects in 38 countries.

What to notice: in Germany the abuse was often run through respected institutions, such as a model school, a youth office and an embassy, and the deadline to prosecute expired while officials did nothing. When reading about any case, ask who received the first report, and what they did in the years before a court acted.

FRA.story:
In 2004 the FBI traced a French surgeon, Joël Le Scouarnec, downloading child abuse images. A French court gave him a four-month suspended sentence in 2005, and nothing restricted his work. Prosecutors did not alert medical authorities, the regional medical body found no breach in 2006, a 2007 warning to the health ministry brought no action, and in 2008 a hospital hired him knowing of the conviction. Between 1989 and 2014 he abused 299 victims, mostly patients, many under anaesthesia or waking from surgery; more than 250 were under 15. He was first convicted for abusing children in 2020, and in May 2025 he received the maximum 20 years. Sixteen years passed between the first report and the first serious action.

The French church was asked to count its own record. A commission chaired by Jean-Marc Sauvé, set up by the bishops in 2018, used a population survey rather than church files and in October 2021 estimated that about 216,000 people were abused as minors by clergy and religious from 1950 to 2020, and about 330,000 including lay church workers. It called the abuse massive and its causes systemic. France also received an accused priest from abroad: the Oblate Fr Johannes Rivoire left Canada's Nunavut for France in 1993, Canada issued warrants in 1998 and 2022, France denied extradition, and he died in France in 2024 without trial. A 2024 review commissioned by his order concluded he had assaulted six Inuit children.

The French state has also moved children itself. From 1963 to 1982 it took 2,015 children from Réunion who had been made wards of the state and sent them to rural mainland departments such as Creuse; in 2014 the National Assembly said the state had failed in its moral responsibility. France received 11,165 Korean children from 1968 to 2008, and in March 2024 a state report admitted the government had long known of "illicit practices of a systemic nature" in intercountry adoption and acted late. In 2007 a French charity, Zoé's Ark, tried to fly 103 children from Chad to France as Darfur orphans; most were Chadian and not orphans, six members were convicted in Chad, and they were pardoned in 2008.

Abroad, six boys aged 9 to 13 told UN staff in 2014 that French soldiers had abused them at a camp in Bangui, Central African Republic, in exchange for food. French judges dismissed the case in 2018 for lack of sufficient charges; no soldier was charged. In 2025 France's share of the abuse material found online by the Internet Watch Foundation rose from 1% to 7%, or 20,475 web addresses.

For a novice, the French cases show that the warnings existed early: an FBI trace, a court conviction, a letter to a ministry, diplomatic archives. The question to ask is why each agency that received a warning passed it on to no one, and who decides whether a country's own soldiers or priests face trial.

UKR.story:
Between 2012 and 2015 investigators from Disability Rights International visited 33 Ukrainian orphanages, boarding schools and institutions for children with disabilities. The anti-trafficking group La Strada Ukraine told them that recruiting children from orphanages into prostitution was "the most typical scheme", and that exploitation inside institutions typically began around age 13, often started by staff. An official of the International Organization for Migration called orphanages a direct feeder to trafficking at home and abroad, with most cases starting in the vocational schools that orphanage leavers attend. Children from Ukraine also travelled as images: Crimea was among the main production sites for films sold by Azov Films in Toronto to customers in more than 50 countries, until Canadian police shut it down in 2013.

Ukraine was a sending country for adoption, with 18,612 children sent abroad from 2003 to 2022, including 10,544 adopted to the United States from 1994 to 2014.

After Russia's full invasion in February 2022, the removal of children became state policy on the Russian side. In May 2022 President Putin signed a decree making it easier to give Ukrainian children Russian citizenship so Russian families could adopt them; Russia kept a register of willing families and paid them per child. Yale's Humanitarian Research Lab reported in February 2023 at least 43 camps in Russia and Crimea holding at least 6,000 Ukrainian children for "re-education". On 17 March 2023 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Vladimir Putin and his children's rights commissioner, Maria Lvova-Belova, charging the unlawful deportation and transfer of children. Ukraine's official Children of War platform counts 20,651 children deported, and about 2,100 were moved to Belarus. The UN Secretary-General verified the abduction of 122 children by Russian forces and authorities; by 2025 two had been reunited and the whereabouts of the rest were unknown. A UN commission found Russian forces committed rape and sexual violence, and Ukraine's prosecutors record 23 children sexually abused.

The war also put Ukraine's own institutions under strain. The 2025 US trafficking report says children evacuated from at least 195 facilities are at high risk, that officials of several state institutions were allegedly complicit or negligent, and that no complicit official had been convicted for the eighth year running. Ukraine convicted 24 traffickers in 2024, six of them with prison terms.

For a novice: children in institutions are the easiest to move, whether by traffickers in peacetime or by an occupying state in war, because no parent is there to object. When a figure like 20,651 appears, ask how many children have been found and returned, and who was responsible for them before they were taken.

NZL.story:
Between 1972 and 1978, 362 children passed through the child and adolescent unit of Lake Alice, a state psychiatric hospital in New Zealand; about half were Māori boys. Survivors described electric shocks without anaesthetic and painful injections given as punishment, and evidence was given of children raped and sexually abused by staff and adult patients. The psychiatrist in charge, Selwyn Leeks, denied abuse and was never criminally charged in New Zealand. The government refused for years to recognise the harm, so survivors took their complaint to the UN Committee Against Torture, which found in 2019 that New Zealand had failed to investigate properly. In December 2024 the government offered NZ$150,000 to each survivor and an apology that named it as torture.

Lake Alice was one part of a wider picture that a Royal Commission spent six years examining. Its final report, Whanaketia, published on 24 July 2024, estimated that 200,000 of about 655,000 people in state and faith-based care between 1950 and 2019 were abused, and that Māori were more likely to be abused. It found that a 2020 church briefing put the share of Catholic clergy accused over 1950 to 1999 at 14%, and singled out Marylands School in Christchurch, run by the St John of God Brothers. It found the church relied on psychiatrists' opinions to move abusers to other ministries, where they reoffended.

Those moves crossed borders. After allegations surfaced in 1977, the St John of God order transferred Brother Bernard McGrath to Australia, where he later faced 252 charges; he was also convicted in New Zealand. The same year Frank Houston, head of the Assemblies of God in New Zealand, who had abused boys there, moved to Sydney. The commission recommended an inquiry into Catholic priests sent to Papua New Guinea after allegations, and a survivor advocate named Fiji as a common destination for clergy transferred from Australia and New Zealand.

New Zealand was also a receiving country: 549 British child migrants arrived between 1948 and 1954, and 559 Korean children were adopted between 1964 and 1984. Since 2005 its law has allowed citizens to be prosecuted for sexual offences against children abroad.

What to notice: New Zealand's numbers became visible only when a commission counted everyone who passed through care, not just the cases that reached court. When an abuser moves overseas, ask whether anyone in the new country was told why.

LKA.story:
In 1987 Sri Lankan police raided a house and found 20 newborn babies and 22 women held in what were described as "prison like conditions". It was one of the "baby farms" that supplied Western adoption agencies through the 1980s. Brokers, hospital doctors and nurses bought or took babies from hospitals and handed them to paid "acting mothers", who posed as birth mothers in court; the adoption records were widely falsified. About 11,000 children are counted in the case, about 4,000 of them sent to the Netherlands and others to the UK, Sweden, Denmark and Germany. Sri Lanka imposed a temporary ban on foreign adoptions after the raid. Thirty years later, in September 2017, a Dutch television documentary brought it back, and the health minister Rajitha Senaratne said on camera that "there were a lot of baby farms back then" and announced an inquiry and a DNA databank. Receiving countries then examined themselves: the Dutch Joustra committee found in 2021 that its officials had known of wrongdoing for years, and the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption; Switzerland acknowledged its authorities' failures in 2020 and 2023.

Sri Lanka also appears as the home country of accused soldiers. From 2004 to 2007 a Sri Lankan army contingent served with the UN mission in Haiti. A UN oversight office concluded that abuse of children by the contingent was "frequent" and happened "at virtually every location" where it was deployed. In 2007, 114 members were accused and 108 were sent home. An Associated Press investigation in 2017 found at least 134 had exploited at least nine children in a sex ring. Because peacekeepers answer to their own country's courts, the case went back to Sri Lanka, where authorities judged the acts "consensual" and no one was jailed. In 2016 Sri Lanka made a one-off ex gratia payment (money given without admitting legal fault) to one victim.

At home, children's homes have shown the same delay. Complaints about a Buddhist monk running a home for war-affected Tamil children in Vavuniya reached the National Child Protection Authority from 2010; he was arrested only in 2013, after protests by local officers, and got bail when the Authority told prosecutors it had no objection. In 2021 two senior probation officials were arrested over a 17-year-old girl made to work as a cook in a children's home near Anuradhapura.

South Asia has no representative survey data on online child sexual exploitation, so how much of that happens in Sri Lanka is not counted. For a novice: Sri Lanka shows how a sending country's records and a receiving country's paperwork can both look clean while children are bought. When soldiers are sent home instead of tried, ask what the home country's court actually did.

ISR.story:
In March 2008, at an ultra-Orthodox girls' school in Melbourne, Australia, a teacher confronted the headmistress, Malka Leifer, about abuse of pupils. The Adass Israel School then arranged and paid for a 1:20 a.m. flight to Israel for Leifer and four of her children, before telling police. Australia issued a warrant in 2014 for 74 offences involving at least eight pupils, and Israel arrested her that August. What followed took almost seven years. Leifer's lawyers sought more than 70 hearings and appeals. Israel's deputy health minister, Yaakov Litzman, pressured ministry staff to change psychiatric evaluations so that she would appear unfit for extradition. In 2019 a court found she had faked mental illness, and on 25 January 2021 she was extradited. A Melbourne jury convicted her of 18 charges including rape on 3 April 2023, and she was sentenced to 15 years. Litzman admitted breach of trust in a 2022 plea deal, resigned from the Knesset, and received eight months' probation and a fine of about US$900.

Israel has received other accused people too: in 2013 a Russian Orthodox priest, Fr Gleb Grozovsky, fled to Israel after a criminal case opened in St Petersburg; he was detained and extradited, and jailed in Russia for 14 years in 2018.

Israel's own early history includes children who vanished from state care. Between 1948 and 1954, more than 1,000 families, mostly immigrants from Yemen and others from the Balkans, North Africa and the Middle East, say babies taken to hospitals disappeared after parents were told they had died; many believe they were given away for adoption. Three government inquiries concluded most of the children died of disease and were buried without their parents being told. In 2021 the government expressed regret and approved NIS 162 million in compensation.

In 2024 a UN commission found that Israeli security forces subjected Palestinians, with men and boys targeted in particular ways, to sexual violence including forced nudity and sexualised torture, and that sexual violence was committed in the 7 October 2023 attacks, when 252 people, including 36 children, were taken hostage.

For a novice: the Leifer case shows that an extradition can be slowed from inside a government, by changing a medical report. When someone accused abroad stays out of reach for years, ask who in the receiving country is involved in the delay, and whether they answer to anyone.

CHN.story:
Between 2002 and 2005, six state orphanages in Hunan province bought babies from traffickers who brought them from Guangdong, and placed nearly 1,000 children with families in China and abroad. When it came out in 2005, 23 officials were fired, three traffickers were sentenced to 15 years and six others to between 3 and 13 years. The orphanages were part of a much larger system. China opened intercountry adoption in 1992 and sent about 160,000 children abroad, peaking at almost 8,000 to the United States in 2005; 87,704 went to the US alone between 1994 and 2014. Reporting in the New Yorker described a programme that came to depend more and more on abduction and trafficking. On 5 September 2024 China ended it, except for adoption by blood relatives or of a stepchild.

China is also the destination at the end of several trafficking routes. Human Rights Watch reported in 2019 that women and girls from Myanmar's Kachin and northern Shan States, many displaced by war, were sold to Chinese families for US$3,000 to 13,000, locked up and raped so they would become pregnant; it said authorities on both sides were "looking away". Brokers sold 629 Pakistani girls and women, many Christian, to Chinese men as brides in 2018 and 2019. The US trafficking report for 2025 describes women and girls from northern Vietnam and Laos lured or abducted to China for forced marriage.

Inside China, as hundreds of thousands of Uyghur and other Muslim adults were detained in Xinjiang, the state built boarding schools and kindergartens with dormitories, including $1.2bn of spending in southern Xinjiang. Records showed more than 400 children in one township had lost both parents to internment or prison. The New York Times reported about 497,000 pupils enrolled in such schools in 2019. This is recorded as a removal of children from their families, not as a sexual-abuse finding.

Very little about online abuse in China reaches international systems. In 2025 the US CyberTipline received 9,406 reports for China, with a population of about 1.4 billion, against 1,933,900 for India. Most US platforms are blocked in China, so the system that counts reports elsewhere cannot see inside it.

For a novice: a low number for China does not mean little abuse; it means the reporting channels used elsewhere do not operate there. Where a state runs the orphanages, the courts and the press, ask who outside the state was able to check what happened to the children.

GRC.story:
After Greece's civil war, between 1950 and 1975, as many as 4,000 Greek-born children were sent abroad for adoption to the United States, the Netherlands and Sweden. Many were called "orphans" of the war or had been born to unmarried mothers. They passed through state institutions and foundling homes, and through US agencies such as AHEPA and intermediaries who arranged "proxy" adoptions, where the adoptive parents never had to appear in Greece. The procedures were rushed and kept confidential, and many adoptees grew up without papers proving where they came from. The Greek state promised an investigation in the late 1950s; it has not been carried out. On 2 May 2025 a new law recognised the adoptees' status, restored a path to Greek citizenship and made it easier for them to see their records. Sweden, one of the receiving countries, published its own inquiry in June 2025, 1,600 pages long, documenting irregularities and illegal acts that state authorities had some knowledge of.

Greece's own institutions for children have also been examined. In March 2011 the Greek Ombudsman reported on the state care centre for children with disabilities at Lechaina: too few doctors and nurses, systematic sedation, residents tied to their beds and wooden cage beds used because of staff shortages, with most children getting no education. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child expressed deep concern in 2012, and a BBC report in 2014 found conditions had barely improved. No sexual-abuse finding was located for Lechaina; this is a record of neglect and restraint.

For a novice: the Greek case shows that it can take 50 years for a state to give adopted children back their own records. When a country promises an investigation, ask whether it ever happened, and whether the people affected can see the files about themselves.

GTM.story:
After Guatemala's civil war ended in 1996, the number of children adopted abroad rose every year. About 98% of adoptions were handled by private notaries, lawyers who managed both the birth mother's side and the adoptive family's side with no court review, and charged $35,000 or more per child. Ninety-seven percent of the children went to the United States, which issued 32,863 visas for children adopted from Guatemala between 1994 and 2014, peaking at 4,728 in 2007. On 11 August 2007 police went into the Casa Quivira adoption home in Antigua after neighbours reported foreigners collecting children every day. They found 46 children, from a few days to three years old. Two lawyers were arrested, and the Attorney General said most of the children lacked proper documents and that his office was checking whether they had been stolen or taken from mothers under pressure. That December Guatemala passed a law meeting the Hague Convention, the international treaty on adoption safeguards, and from 1 January 2008 it stopped new adoptions to the US. A 2010 report by the commission known as CICIG studied 153 cases and found 78% broke the law in some way.

Children who stayed in state care faced a different danger. About 700 children lived at the Hogar Seguro Virgen de la Asunción, a state home built for 500. Most had committed no crime. Girls protested overcrowding and alleged sexual abuse by staff, prosecutors recommended closing the home, and in November 2016 the Human Rights Ombudsman asked the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights for protection, citing a trafficking network recruiting children from it. After an escape on 7 March 2017, police brought a group of girls back and locked them in a room. The next day one set a mattress on fire; 41 girls died, and the officers guarding the door did not let them out. On 12 August 2025 a judge convicted six former officials, with sentences of 6 to 25 years, and ordered an investigation of former President Jimmy Morales.

Guatemalan children are also trafficked north, through Mexico to the United States, according to the 2025 US trafficking report.

For a novice: Guatemala shows how a payment of $35,000 per child, with no judge checking, creates a market for children. When an adoption system closes, ask where the brokers went next, and who was responsible for the children left behind in state homes.

JPN.story:
In 1965 a Japanese weekly, Weekly Sankei, published the earliest cited report about Johnny Kitagawa, founder of the Johnny & Associates talent agency. In 1999 the magazine Shūkan Bunshun ran a series alleging that he sexually abused boys who trained with his agency hoping to become pop singers. Kitagawa sued for defamation and won a judgment in 2002, but higher courts upheld the magazine's reporting on the abuse in 2003, and the Supreme Court rejected his appeal in 2004. Japan's mainstream media barely covered it; journalists said the agency controlled which stars appeared on their programmes. Kitagawa died in 2019 and was never charged.

The silence broke in 2023, after a BBC documentary in March and a former trainee's public statements in April. An external investigation set up by the agency concluded on 29 August 2023 that Kitagawa had abused minors for decades. A UN Human Rights Council working group visited Japan that July. The company admitted the abuse in September, split into a new talent agency and a company called Smile-Up to handle compensation; 478 people came forward as victims, and 545 were later paid. In March 2024 Smile-Up's chief executive said he believed two more abusers had worked at the agency. Twenty-four years passed between the 1999 series and the first official action.

Japan changed its criminal law in June 2023, extending the deadline to prosecute rape from 10 to 15 years and raising the age of consent from 13 to 16. A survivor group, Spring, said it was not enough. Since 1999 Japanese nationals can be prosecuted at home for child prostitution and child abuse images produced abroad.

Japan also hosts foreign troops. In September 1995 three US servicemen from Camp Hansen on Okinawa abducted and raped a 12-year-old girl. They were tried in a Japanese court and in 1996 sentenced to between six and a half and seven years, and the case set off mass protests against the bases.

For a novice: the Kitagawa case was not hidden; it was published and upheld in court, then ignored for two decades. When powerful people are named in court and nothing changes, ask who depended on them for business, and who decided not to report it.

KEN.story:
In 2020 reporters from BBC Africa Eye spent a year in Nairobi following a trade in babies. They found children snatched from homeless mothers on the street and sold for about £350 to £550, and illegal street clinics selling newborns; one offered an unborn child for about £315 while paying the mother £70. At Mama Lucy Kibaki Hospital, run by the government, a clinical social worker sold an abandoned two-week-old boy to undercover reporters for 300,000 shillings (£2,000), using real transfer paperwork. The reporters took all the children to a children's home. When the story ran in November 2020, the official appeared to still have his job and the clinic appeared to still be operating.

On the coast, a 2006 study by UNICEF and the Kenyan government found that Italian, German and Swiss tourists made up 44 per cent of the clients of exploited children, and Kenyans 38 per cent. The 2025 US trafficking report cites a 2023 study estimating more than 2,000 children exploited in Kilifi and Kwale counties, increasingly in private villas and holiday homes rather than hotels. It also describes rings moving girls from Uganda's Karamoja region to Nairobi, and notes concerns about officials taking part, with no action reported against them. Some foreign offenders are prosecuted at home: Keith Morris was jailed in the UK for 18.5 years for offences against children in Kenya, one of about eight UK prosecutions for offences abroad since 1997.

Kenya is also the setting of a false accusation. In May 2011 the Irish broadcaster RTÉ's documentary "Mission to Prey" said an Irish priest, Fr Kevin Reynolds, had fathered a child with a minor in Kenya. It was untrue. RTÉ apologised, paid him a large libel settlement, and its director general called it one of its gravest mistakes.

For a novice: the trade in Kenya moved from hotels to private villas, and in one hospital it used official forms. A false story, like RTÉ's, can make real cases harder to believe. When reading a report, ask whether it was tested, and whether the officials it names were ever investigated.

PER.story:
In 1964, in Lima, a Spanish Jesuit named Alfonso Pedrajas abused a minor for the first time. He then settled in neighbouring Bolivia, where he abused more than 80 minors at Jesuit schools. In 1978 he confessed to a superior, who covered it up. Peru has also been on the receiving end of the same kind of move: in 2010 a Marist Brother in Chile, Abel Pérez, confessed to his superiors that he had abused minors, and the Marist Brothers transferred him to Peru.

Peru's main reckoning so far came from inside a Catholic movement rather than from the state. In 2016 the Catholic movement Sodalitium Christianae Vitae commissioned an inquiry into its founder, Luis Figari. Its report, in February 2017, found that he had sexually abused at least one minor and others.

Today the visible exploitation is tied to tourism and to mining and logging. The 2025 US trafficking report says tourists from the United States and Europe exploit children in Cusco, Lima and the Peruvian Amazon. In Loreto, criminal groups take foreign tourists by boat to remote places on the Amazon River where women and children are exploited. Peruvian, Venezuelan and Bolivian women and girls are lured to mining and logging camps, and the Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua has reportedly moved trafficking victims from the Colombian border city of Cúcuta to Peru. Peruvian courts convicted 59 traffickers in 2024. Two police officers were charged with crimes against trafficking victims, and the report says corruption remained a significant concern. Peru also sends children abroad for adoption: 2,049 between 2003 and 2022.

For a novice: Peru shows abusers being moved across borders by religious orders in both directions, and an inquiry paid for by the movement whose founder was accused. When a church body investigates itself, ask who chose the investigators and whether police were told. In remote river and mining areas, ask who is there to check on children.

SDN.story:
Since war broke out in Sudan in 2023, an independent UN fact-finding mission has collected accounts from women and girls across the country. It found rape and gang rape were widespread, carried out mostly by men in the uniform of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and allied militias, with some cases by the Sudanese Armed Forces. The victims included girls as young as 8. The mission found that the RSF's abduction and detention of women and girls for sexual purposes amounted to sexual slavery. The UN Secretary-General verified sexual violence against 114 girls in 2023, 57 of them by the RSF, and against 74 children in 2024, 54 by the RSF and 9 by militia linked to it. The UN now lists the RSF for the rape and abduction of children. Soldiers from a neighbouring country appear in the same records: the UN attributed 4 of 35 verified cases of sexual violence against girls aged 12 to 17 in Sudan to Chad's national army.

Sudan is also a destination. The 2025 US trafficking report says Ethiopian girls are exploited in domestic servitude and sex trafficking in neighbouring countries, particularly Djibouti and Sudan, sometimes kept under control with drugs, and that reports of officials taking part continued.

These UN counts are what has been verified in a war zone, not the total. The Middle East and North Africa region has no representative survey data on online sexual exploitation of children, so that side is not counted at all.

For a novice: in Sudan the main abusers named by the UN are armed forces, the same groups that hold power over the territory where the children live. When you see a verified number such as 114 girls, ask how many cases the UN could not reach, and which court, if any, can try a commander for it.

DOM.story:
In 2008 a Polish archbishop, Józef Wesołowski, arrived in Santo Domingo as the Pope's ambassador, called a nuncio. In August 2013, amid allegations that he had abused minors, the Vatican recalled him to Rome. Dominican prosecutors opened a criminal investigation on 4 September 2013, after he had already left. The Holy See told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow his extradition. A church tribunal found him guilty and he was removed from the priesthood in 2014. In June 2015 a Vatican prosecutor charged him with abusing children in the Dominican Republic from 2008 to 2013 and with possessing child abuse images. He was found dead in his Vatican rooms in August 2015, before trial.

A Polish priest who worked in the Dominican Republic, Fr Wojciech Gil, was suspended in May 2013 and went home to Poland, which has no extradition treaty with the Dominican Republic. Here the move did not end the case: Polish police arrested him in February 2014 using Dominican evidence, and on 25 March 2015 a court in Wołomin sentenced him to seven years for abusing six minors in the Dominican Republic and two in Poland.

The country's north coast has drawn foreign offenders. US men have been prosecuted under the PROTECT Act, a US law that lets American citizens be tried at home for abusing children abroad, for abusing boys and girls in Puerto Plata and Sosúa, and US and Dominican agents ran joint operations in tourist towns. After the 2010 earthquake in Haiti, members of a US group called New Life Children's Refuge tried to take 33 children across the border into the Dominican Republic.

For a novice: both men left the country where the children lived before or as police began to act. Gil was tried because Polish police used the Dominican evidence; Wesołowski was charged only by the Vatican, which had recalled him, and he died before trial. When an accused official leaves before police are called, ask who decided the timing.

CZE.story:
In 2000 and 2001 a Czech court found Fr František Merta, a priest in the Archdiocese of Olomouc, guilty of abusing more than 20 boys. He received a two-year suspended sentence, meaning he did not go to prison unless he offended again. The archbishop, Jan Graubner, is alleged to have failed to report him and to have moved him from parish to parish when problems arose.

Czechia also appears as a place where abuse images were made. A Czech photographer and a Swedish partner distributed images of about 70 children to buyers in the European Union and Canada, and Europol announced by 2014 that the network had been dismantled.

Its history includes the Nazi occupation, when Nazi Germany seized children judged "racially valuable" in occupied countries and placed them with German families under new identities. At the Nuremberg RuSHA trial in 1948, 13 officials of the SS offices that ran it were convicted.

For a novice: the Merta case is small in number of documents but shows the common pattern of moving a priest instead of reporting him. When a court gives a suspended sentence for abuse of more than 20 children, ask whether he was still allowed to work with children afterwards, and who decided where he was sent.

NER.story:
In 2024 the UN verified the abduction of 202 children in Niger, 102 of them girls. Most, 163, were taken by perpetrators the UN could not identify. Thirty-five were taken by the armed group JAS, two by ISWAP and two by ISGS. The UN also verified sexual violence against five girls that year. In 2023 it verified sexual violence against 8 girls, and in one of those cases the perpetrator was Niger's own security forces.

These figures are only the cases UN monitors could confirm in an armed conflict, where access is limited and many families cannot report. Beyond them, the record is mostly empty. West and Central Africa have no representative surveys on online sexual exploitation of children, so there is no estimate of how many children in Niger are abused that way.

For a novice: when the largest group of abductors is "unidentified", it means the UN confirmed that children were taken but could not say by whom, which makes it hard to hold anyone to account. A blank on this map for Niger is a sign that nobody has counted, not that nothing happened.

BOL.story:
In 1964 a Spanish Jesuit, Alfonso Pedrajas, abused a minor for the first time in Lima, Peru. He then settled in Bolivia and abused more than 80 minors at Jesuit schools there. In 1978 he confessed to a superior in his order, who covered it up instead of reporting him. Bolivia received an abuser who had already offended in another country, and his order did not tell the authorities.

The 2025 US trafficking report describes a different set of offenders. Foreign visitors exploited children in rural Indigenous communities in northern La Paz department, in and around Rurrenabaque, and in Santa Cruz, as well as in tourist areas of La Paz and Beni. The making of abuse material for sale online is rising in Cochabamba, El Alto and Santa Cruz, sometimes involving parents. Bolivian women and girls are trafficked to Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Panama and Peru, and the Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua is reported to be active in the country.

For a novice: the Pedrajas case is about what an order did after a confession: it kept the secret for decades. In remote communities that see foreign tourists, ask who checks on children, and whether the visitors' home countries prosecute their citizens for what they do abroad.

IRQ.story:
On 3 August 2014 the Islamic State, known as ISIS, attacked Sinjar, in northern Iraq. Its fighters moved captured Yazidis, members of a religious minority, in an organised way, by bus and truck, to holding sites: in Tal Afar, in Mosul at Badoush prison and the Galaxy wedding hall, and in Baaj. From there, women and girls were taken onward to Raqqa in Syria. The UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria reported in June 2016, in a report titled "They came to destroy", that ISIS had committed genocide. It found women and girls, some as young as nine, were sold at markets and held as sexual slaves, and boys were forced into ISIS training camps. At that date more than 3,200 Yazidi women and children were still held, mostly in Syria, and thousands remain missing.

This is the record of a single armed group using the sale of children as a planned part of its campaign. It is not a full count of child abuse in Iraq. The Middle East and North Africa region has no representative surveys on online sexual exploitation of children, so that side is not measured.

For a novice: the holding sites, the transport and the markets show that the taking of Yazidi children was organised, not random violence. When a figure like 3,200 appears, remember it counts those still held in 2016; ask how many have been found since, and who is searching for the rest.

LBR.story:
When Liberia's civil war ended in 2003, the number of private orphanages rose from 40 to 120. The UN mission in Liberia found orphanages that were run for profit and had no accreditation. In 2005 the Hannah B. Williams Orphanage in Monrovia was closed, and 89 of its 102 "orphans" were returned to their families. A 2007 report by UNICEF and the adoption agency Holt International found that many children had entered the adoption pipeline through fraud, including false promises to birth parents. The United States issued 1,553 visas for children adopted from Liberia between 1994 and 2014, peaking at 353 in 2006. Canada placed a moratorium, a temporary stop, on adoptions from Liberia.

Little else is counted. West and Central Africa have no representative surveys on online sexual exploitation of children, so there is no estimate for Liberia.

For a novice: the jump from 40 to 120 orphanages after a war is the signal. When a country's orphanage count triples after a war, ask how many of the children have living parents, and who is paid when a child is placed abroad.

CMR.story:
In 2023 UN monitors verified sexual violence against 17 girls in Cameroon. Ten of those cases were attributed to the Cameroon Armed Forces, the country's own army, six to perpetrators the UN could not identify, and one to the armed group JAS. In 2024 the UN verified sexual violence against 6 more girls, one of them by the armed forces, and the abduction of 50 children. These are only the cases that UN monitors in conflict areas could confirm.

Beyond those figures, the record is mostly blank. West and Central Africa have no representative surveys on online sexual exploitation of children, so no one has estimated how many children in Cameroon are abused that way.

For a novice: in 2023, 10 of the 17 verified cases of sexual violence against girls in Cameroon were attributed to the national army. When the accused are state soldiers, ask whether the state has tried any of them, and who else could.

JEY.story:
From 2007 to 2010 police on the island of Jersey ran an investigation called Operation Rectangle, centred on a former children's home, Haut de la Garenne. An Independent Jersey Care Inquiry followed and heard from about 450 people connected with the island's care system since 1945. It reported in July 2017. It found that the States of Jersey, the island's government, had been "an ineffectual and neglectful substitute parent" for children in its care, that its child-welfare law was decades behind, and that some children in care might still be at risk. It found the authorities had failed to build a culture of openness, which fed beliefs that officials were colluding and covering up, and it described a "small island culture" that nobody challenged. It recommended that the Haut de la Garenne buildings be demolished. The Chief Minister, Ian Gorst, apologised: "We failed children who needed our care."

For a novice: on a small island the people who run care homes, the police and the government often know each other, and the inquiry found that this closeness was never countered. When a place is that small, ask who outside it checks on the children in state care.

TWN.story:
In February 2011 Thai police entered two houses in Bangkok and freed 14 Vietnamese women, half of them pregnant. A company called Baby 101 had taken their passports and was taking orders from childless couples for newborn babies. Four of the women said they had been tricked, and Thailand's health minister said some appeared to have been raped. A Taiwanese woman said to run the operation was charged with human trafficking. Taiwan appears on this map through her case, and as a sending country for adoption: 4,289 children were sent abroad from Taiwan between 2003 and 2022, and that route is still open.

For a novice: Baby 101 took orders for babies and held the women who would give birth to them, with their passports confiscated. When a country keeps sending children abroad for adoption, ask who checks where each child came from and what was paid.

PNG.story:
Papua New Guinea appears on this map as a place where abusers were sent. In 2024 New Zealand's Royal Commission into Abuse in Care found that the Catholic Church had transferred abusers to other ministries instead of reporting them, and it recommended a separate investigation into Catholic priests who were sent to Papua New Guinea after abuse allegations were made against them. The commission did not state how many priests were sent, and no inquiry into what happened after they arrived appears in the sources.

For a novice: when an abuser is moved overseas, the children in the new country are the ones put at risk, usually without anyone there being told. The question to ask is where each of those priests went in Papua New Guinea, and whether anyone there has looked.

KGZ.story:
Kyrgyzstan appears on this map as one of the countries along the moving route of intercountry adoption. In 2009 it suspended adoptions of its children by foreign families, and in April 2010 the US State Department issued an alert telling American families. This fits a wider pattern: adoption agencies moved from one sending country to the next, from South Korea to Romania, Guatemala, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia, and each was closed after inquiries found children bought, stolen or registered as orphans. The sources on this map do not say what problems led to Kyrgyzstan's suspension, and no case from Kyrgyzstan is recorded.

For a novice: a suspension tells you a government saw a reason to stop, but not what the reason was. The question to ask is what was found, and which country the agencies turned to next.

GUM.story:
In 2016 Guam, a US territory in the Pacific, opened a permanent window for old abuse claims, meaning survivors could sue no matter how long ago the abuse happened. Most survivors disclose decades later, after the usual legal deadline to sue has passed. Once Guam's deadline was lifted, claims against the island's Catholic archdiocese rose to nearly 280. On 15 and 16 January 2019 the archdiocese filed for bankruptcy, a court process that puts all claims into one pot to be settled at once. Its plan in January 2020 offered $21 million, and it sold a property in Yona for $6.1 million. The former archbishop, Anthony Apuron, was found guilty in a church trial in 2018 and 2019; that was a canonical trial, under church law, not a criminal court. Guam follows the US pattern, where 40 Catholic dioceses and orders filed for bankruptcy from 2004 to 2025.

For a novice: across the US, several dioceses filed for bankruptcy within hours or days of a trial, a deposition or a new law. When a church files soon after a deadline is lifted, ask how the settlement compares with the number of claims, and what the claimants gave up to receive it.

GNQ.story:
Equatorial Guinea has no documented case on this map. That is not evidence that children there are safe. Childlight, a research centre that pulls together surveys on child sexual exploitation, based its 2026 update on representative surveys from only 60 countries, and West and Central Africa have none on technology-facilitated abuse. The UN's 2024 global trafficking report covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied 2023 data. Where no one runs a survey and no inquiry is held, nothing appears on a map, and the country is colored by estimate only.

For a novice: a blank country here means a missing record. The question to ask is who would collect the data, and why it has not been done.

JOR.story:
Jordan has no documented case on this map. The reason is a gap in the data rather than a finding of safety. Childlight, a research centre that pulls together surveys on child sexual exploitation, based its 2026 update on representative surveys from only 60 countries, and the Middle East and North Africa region has none on technology-facilitated abuse. The UN's 2024 global trafficking report covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied 2023 data. Without surveys or inquiries, abuse that is not reported to police does not appear anywhere, and the country is colored by estimate only.

For a novice: a blank country means nobody has measured. The question to ask is whether anyone in the country has surveyed children directly, and if not, who could.

QAT.story:
Qatar has no documented case on this map. That reflects the record, not the children. Childlight, a research centre that pulls together surveys on child sexual exploitation, based its 2026 update on representative surveys from only 60 countries, and the Middle East and North Africa region has none on technology-facilitated abuse. The UN's 2024 global trafficking report covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied 2023 data. When there is no survey and no inquiry, only cases that reach police or the press could appear, and none are in the sources for Qatar.

For a novice: a blank country is a gap to ask about. The useful question is whether anyone outside the government has been able to collect data on children there.

GHA.story:
Ghana has no documented case on this map. That is a gap in the record. Childlight, a research centre that pulls together surveys on child sexual exploitation, based its 2026 update on representative surveys from only 60 countries, and West and Central Africa have none on technology-facilitated abuse. The UN's 2024 global trafficking report covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied 2023 data. Without surveys or inquiries, abuse that is never reported to police leaves no trace, and the country is colored by estimate only.

For a novice: a blank country means the counting has not been done. The question to ask is who would fund a survey of children in Ghana, and why none appears yet.

TKM.story:
In 2025 the US CyberTipline, the main international system that collects reports of child abuse material found online, received 591 reports for Turkmenistan. On this map Turkmenistan is listed among the countries from which almost no reports reach the international systems, so the number shows how little the reporting channels see, not how much abuse happens. The system has wider blind spots too: in 2025, 14% of its 23.4 million reports could not be placed in any country, and North Korea had 12. No case from Turkmenistan is recorded on this map, and the country is colored by estimate only.

For a novice: a low number of reports can mean the reporting channels do not reach a country. The question to ask is which platforms people there use, and whether those platforms report anything at all.
